schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}; all entries here have '867': false.
schema_notes.replacement_candidates: List of exactly 3 associated natural feature names and historical tribal/ethnonym names (>=1 tribe per barony) usable as localisation replacements.
schema_notes.name: Clean display name of the replacement candidate (Wikipedia disambiguation suffixes extracted to disambiguation_note).
schema_notes.disambiguation_note: Optional disambiguator extracted from parenthetical/comma qualifiers (e.g. 'Liao', 'Orkney', 'river'); null if none.
schema_notes.localisation_stem: Clean CK3-ready toponym stem stripped of redundant generic English feature suffixes/prefixes ('River', 'Mount', 'Lake', 'people', etc.) while preserving meaningful compounds.
schema_notes.attestation_basis: Historicity classification distinguishing genuinely pre-867/pre-literate entities from medieval post-867 ethnogeneses: attested_pre_867 | indigenous_pre_literate | attested_867_to_1066 | attested_1066_to_1178.
schema_notes.valid_for_bookmarks: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'} indicating whether the replacement candidate is historically non-anachronistic for that bookmark (true for both attested_pre_867 and indigenous_pre_literate; bookmark-gated for attested_867_to_1066 and attested_1066_to_1178).
schema_notes.candidates_with_multilingual_variants: Count of replacement candidates having more than 1 distinct language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 or documented proto-stage code) across language_variants.
schema_notes.language_variants_policy: Include core local/classical forms plus regionally scoped vernaculars and genuinely distinct exonyms; exclude out-of-region exonym padding and redundant eng copies (eng is retained only when no non-English variant exists). Uses ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 language_code values plus documented Wiktionary proto/stage codes (sla-pro, gem-pro, cel-pro, cel-bry, urj-fin-pro); reconstructed proto/ancient forms carry a leading '*'.
schema_notes.language_variants: List of cultural/historical name forms: {form, native_script, language, language_code, notes}. form is always clean Latin script (or romanization) suitable for CK3 localisation; native_script holds the native non-Latin script form or null when the language natively uses Latin script.
schema_notes.relationship: Prose description of the geographical, ecological, or historical relationship between the replacement entity and the audited barony.
schema_notes.etymology_notes: Linguistic etymology, onomastic origin, or geographic/ethnographic characterization of the replacement entity (incorporating attested onomastic notes from language variants where documented).

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Confluence of the Odet and Steïr rivers

replacement_candidates.name: Odet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary coastal river flowing through Quimper, where its confluence with the Steir gives the city its Breton name Kemper ('confluence').
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Pre-Breton/Celtic hydronymic root preserved in medieval Breton and French records; no exact single earliest charter year established.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from a generic Celtic or pre-Celtic hydronymic root *od- ('water, watercourse') with a diminutive or collective suffix.

replacement_candidates.name: Cornouaille
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical southwestern Breton province and bishopric whose traditional capital is Quimper.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: First attested between 852 and 857 CE in records mentioning Anaweten, bishop of Cornouaille.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Cognate with British Cornwall (from the Brittonic tribe Cornovii, 'people of the horn/peninsula'), brought by early medieval Brittonic migrants.

replacement_candidates.name: Osismii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe inhabiting Finistère and western Brittany, including the Quimper basin.

language_variants.notes: Attested as Osismi by Caesar and Ossismos by Pliny
Gaulish form reflected in Greek Osismioi (Strabo)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Julius Caesar in the mid-1st century BCE (circa 57 BCE) and Strabo in the early 1st century CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *uxsamos / *osismos ('the highest' or 'the furthest/outermost'), referring to their position at the western extremity of Gaul.

replacement_candidates.name: Scorff
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal river entering the Rade de Lorient alongside the Blavet, forming the eastern waterfront of Lorient.

language_variants.notes: Attested in genitive as Pons Scorvi in 1280 CE

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Scorvi in 1280 CE (in the place-name Pons Scorvi, modern Pont-Scorff).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Breton skorf ('outlet/discharge of a pond or millpond'), denoting a hydrological outflow channel.

replacement_candidates.name: Blavet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Breton river whose estuary joins the Scorff to form the Rade de Lorient.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Breton hydronym preserved in regional charters; exact earliest attestation year not established.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attributed either to Breton blavet ('gushing or running water') or to a pre-Celtic root meaning 'marshy'.

replacement_candidates.name: Veneti
replacement_candidates.relationship: Seafaring Armorican Gaulish tribe inhabiting the Morbihan coast, including the Lorient estuary.

language_variants.notes: Attested by Caesar, Livy, and Pliny

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (mid-1st century BCE, circa 57–56 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from Proto-Celtic *wenetoi ('kinsmen, friendly ones, or beloved'), from Indo-European *wen- ('to desire, love').

replacement_candidates.name: Léon
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical northwestern Breton province and bishopric whose traditional capital is Saint-Pol-de-Léon.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in the 9th-century Life of Saint Paul Aurelian (884 CE) as pagus Legionensis / Castellum Leonense.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Traditionally linked to Latin legio ('legion', via a Roman military post Castellum Legionense) or to an ancient Brittonic/Gaulish toponym.

replacement_candidates.name: Penzé
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal river and ria forming the eastern natural boundary of Saint-Pol-de-Léon at the entrance to the Bay of Morlaix.

language_variants.notes: Breton form (also Penzes in older orthography)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Breton coastal toponym/hydronym recorded in medieval and early modern Finistère documents.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Associated with Breton penzes ('shipwreck, flotsam') or Breton penn ('head, end') combined with a coastal/estuarine element.

replacement_candidates.name: Osismii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe inhabiting all of Finistère, including the Pays de Léon and Saint-Pol-de-Léon.

language_variants.notes: Gaulish form reflected in Greek Osismioi

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *uxsamos / *osismos ('the highest' or 'the outermost'), referring to the western tip of Armorica.

replacement_candidates.name: Chère
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary 65 km river flowing through the marshy valley in which Châteaubriant developed before joining the Vilaine.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Pre-Romance hydronym recorded in medieval Breton-march charters; exact earliest year not established.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from a pre-Indo-European or Celtic root *kar- ('stone, rocky bed'), common to rocky-bed rivers in Gaul.

replacement_candidates.name: Pays de la Mée
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical Breton pays in northern Loire-Atlantique whose chief town is Châteaubriant.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval regional name preserved in local parish names such as Ercé-en-Lamée and Soudan-en-la-Mée.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Latin media (terra), meaning 'middle land', referring to its buffer position between Nantes, Rennes, and Anjou.

replacement_candidates.name: Namnetes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish tribe of the lower Loire and Loire-Atlantique whose northern territory encompassed the Châteaubriant area.

language_variants.notes: Reflected in Greek Namniton (Polybius, 2nd century BCE)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Namniton by Polybius in the 2nd century BCE and as Namnetes by Julius Caesar in the mid-1st century BCE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Possibly connected to Gaulish *nanto- ('valley, stream') or *nam- ('bent, winding'), referring to the lower Loire valley.

replacement_candidates.name: Gouët
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary 47 km coastal river flowing through Saint-Brieuc into the Bay of Saint-Brieuc at Le Légué.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Derived from Old Breton guoaeth (5th–11th century CE) and Middle Breton goaz.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Breton guoaeth (Modern Breton gwazh, cognate with Middle Welsh gwyth), meaning 'stream, watercourse, channel'.

replacement_candidates.name: Penthièvre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Traditional Breton pays and historical archdeaconry of the Diocese of Saint-Brieuc lying east and south of Saint-Brieuc.

language_variants.notes: Attested as Pentavro in 1144 CE and Penthevria in 1212 CE

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Pentavro in 1144 CE and Penthevria in 1212 CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Breton penn ('head, end') and a second element possibly related to Old Breton *tevr / *tavr or a regional tribal/geographical name.

replacement_candidates.name: Coriosolites
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe inhabiting eastern Côtes-d'Armor, including the Bay of Saint-Brieuc.

language_variants.notes: Attested by Caesar (also Coriosvelites in Pliny)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (mid-1st century BCE) and Pliny the Elder (1st century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *corio- ('army, host, tribe') combined with *sol- / *suel- (possibly 'watchful' or 'commanding').

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Trégor (Breton Treger, land of the three tribes/pagi)

replacement_candidates.name: Jaudy
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal river and ria bordering Tréguier on the east, where it meets the Guindy to form the Tréguier estuary.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Breton coastal river name preserved in regional toponyms such as Pommerit-Jaudy and La Roche-Jaudy.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Shares a Breton hydronymic ending -dy with the neighboring Guindy, likely from an old Brittonic water/estuary compound.

replacement_candidates.name: Trégor
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical northwestern Breton province and bishopric whose capital is Tréguier.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in early medieval Breton Latin sources as Pagus Tricurius / Trecorum (9th century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Brittonic/Gaulish *Tri-corii ('three armies/hosts/districts', cognate with Cornish Trigg).

replacement_candidates.name: Osismii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe whose territory extended across western Côtes-d'Armor, including the Trégor and Tréguier.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Julius Caesar in the mid-1st century BCE (circa 57 BCE) and Strabo in the early 1st century CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *uxsamos / *osismos ('the highest' or 'the outermost').

replacement_candidates.name: Rance
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major coastal river and tidal estuary on whose right bank Saint-Malo and ancient Alet sit.

language_variants.notes: Attested as Renc, Rentia (9th c. CE) and Rinctus/Rinctius (9th–10th c. CE)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in the 9th century CE as Renc and Rentia, and in the 9th–10th centuries CE as Rinctus and Rinctius.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from a pre-Romance (Celtic or pre-Celtic) hydronymic root *renk- / *rink-.

replacement_candidates.name: Clos Poulet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical peninsula and pagus (Pagus Aleti) bounded by the Rance estuary, the English Channel, and the marshes of Dol, encompassing Saint-Malo.

language_variants.notes: Medieval Latin form (also Poëlet, Pavelet in 1032 CE)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Pavelet in 1032 CE, Pohelet in 1040 CE, and Poëlet in the 11th century CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Alteration of Breton Pou Alet ('land/pagus of Alet', from Latin pagus + Aletum, the Gallo-Roman predecessor of Saint-Malo).

replacement_candidates.name: Coriosolites
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe whose territory included the Rance estuary and the Gallo-Roman fortified port of Alet (Saint-Malo).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (mid-1st century BCE) and Pliny the Elder (1st century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *corio- ('army, warband') combined with a second element *sol- / *suel-.

replacement_candidates.name: Forêt du Mesnil
replacement_candidates.relationship: State forest (603 ha) immediately north of Combourg along the historic road connecting Combourg to Mesnil-Roc'h and Dol.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Forested tract containing Neolithic megaliths (La Maison des Fées); medieval name derives from Old French mesnil.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old French mesnil (Late Latin *mansionile, 'small rural estate or farmstead').

replacement_candidates.name: Poudouvre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Traditional northeastern Upper Breton pagus bordering the Combourg-Dinan corridor in the historical Diocese of Saint-Malo.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Poodoria in 1184 CE, Podourie in 1231 CE, and Poudouvre in 1280 CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Breton pou ('country', from Latin pagus) + daou dour ('two waters'), meaning 'land between two rivers' (the Rance and Arguenon).

replacement_candidates.name: Redones
replacement_candidates.relationship: Armorican Gaulish tribe inhabiting Ille-et-Vilaine (centered on Rennes), whose northern territory included Combourg.

language_variants.notes: Attested as R(h)edones by Caesar and Pliny

replacement_candidates.name: Cézallier Massif
replacement_candidates.relationship: Volcanic highland plateau bordering the western edge of Haute-Loire directly adjacent to Mercœur and the Alagnon gorge.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in regional Auvergnat toponymy; no surviving Classical attestation.

replacement_candidates.name: Alagnon

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Celtic or Gaulish hydronym built on the root *al- / *alan-.

replacement_candidates.name: Arverni
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish tribe whose Brivadois territory in northwestern Haute-Loire encompassed the plateau of Mercœur.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Livy (27.39) in 207 BCE during Hasdrubal's crossing of Gaul, as well as in 121 BCE (Bituitus) and Caesar's Gallic Wars (52 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *are- ('near') + *werno- ('alder tree').

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Hill of Montpensier

replacement_candidates.name: Limagne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fertile alluvial plain of the Allier in northern Auvergne, directly overlooked by the hill of Montpensier.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin form (Gregory of Tours)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Limania in the 6th century CE by Gregory of Tours.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Latin limus ('silt, mud') or a pre-Latin/Gaulish root *lim- ('marsh, lake'), referring to the ancient drained lakebed of the plain.

replacement_candidates.name: Allier
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river draining the Limagne plain immediately east of Montpensier.

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish or pre-Celtic *Elaver / *Elavris.

replacement_candidates.name: Arverni
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish tribe whose core fertile heartland in the northern Limagne included Montpensier.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Livy (27.39) in 207 BCE during Hasdrubal's crossing of Gaul, as well as in 121 BCE (Bituitus) and Caesar's Gallic Wars (52 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *are- ('near') + *werno- ('alder tree').

replacement_candidates.name: Dore
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river flowing directly through the valley and town of Ambert.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Auvergnat charters as Dora; pre-Celtic origin.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From the widespread pre-Celtic/Gaulish hydronymic root *dura / *dor- ('water, river').

replacement_candidates.name: Livradois
replacement_candidates.relationship: Natural and historical upland region of eastern Auvergne whose chief town is Ambert.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 10th-century CE Auvergnat cartularies as pagus Liberatensis / Livradois.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From a Gallo-Roman estate or territorial name *Liberatum / Liberatensis (Latin personal name Liberatus + suffix -ensis).

replacement_candidates.name: Arverni
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish tribe whose eastern territory in the Dore valley and Livradois encompassed Ambert.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Livy (27.39) in 207 BCE during Hasdrubal's crossing of Gaul, as well as in 121 BCE (Bituitus) and Caesar's Gallic Wars (52 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *are- ('near') + *werno- ('alder tree').

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Volcanic peak (Mount Anis / Podium)

replacement_candidates.name: Velay
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical province and volcanic upland region of the Massif Central whose capital is Le Puy-en-Velay.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin pagus name; also 'Vellaicum' — Medieval Latin variant.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Derived from the Vellavii (1st century BCE); attested as pagus Vellavus / Vellavensis in Merovingian sources (6th century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Directly continues the ethnonym of the Gaulish tribe Vellavii.

replacement_candidates.name: Borne
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing directly through Le Puy-en-Velay (past the Rocher Saint-Michel d'Aiguilhe) into the Loire.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Velay charters as Borna; pre-Celtic origin.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From a pre-Celtic or Gaulish hydronymic root *born- ('spring, bubbling water, hollow').

replacement_candidates.name: Vellavii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish client tribe of the Arverni inhabiting the Velay, whose Gallo-Roman capital Ruessium preceded Le Puy-en-Velay.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico (52 BCE) as clients of the Arverni.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Celtic *wello- ('good, noble, superior'), meaning 'the noble ones' or 'the best'.

replacement_candidates.name: Garraf Massif
replacement_candidates.relationship: Karstic coastal mountain massif rising directly behind Sitges.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: The toponym Garraf is attested in early 11th-century CE Catalan documents.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Uncertain origin; variously linked to a pre-Roman/Iberian root *gar-/*kar- ('rock, crag', fitting the karst massif) or Arabic garraf ('waterwheel/ravine').

replacement_candidates.name: Riera de Ribes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal Mediterranean stream flowing into the sea at Sitges.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Catalan hydronym named after Sant Pere de Ribes (attested as Ribas from the 10th century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Catalan riera ('seasonal Mediterranean watercourse') + Ribes (Latin ripa, 'riverbank').

replacement_candidates.name: Cessetani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe of the Tarragona–Penedès coast (ancient Subur, associated with Sitges, lay along the Cessetani–Laietani frontier).

language_variants.notes: Iberian coin legend of their capital

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in accounts of the Second Punic War (218 BCE, Polybius/Livy) and on Iberian bronze coins inscribed Kese.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym derived from their chief city Kese (Cissa, near Tarraco) with the Latinized suffix -tani.

replacement_candidates.name: Ausetani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe whose chief settlement Ausa became modern Vic.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Livy for 218 BCE, by Pliny the Elder, and on Iberian coins reading Ausesken (2nd–1st centuries BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym derived from their capital Ausa (modern Vic, also yielding Osona) with Iberian plural/gentilic -sken / Latin -tani.

replacement_candidates.name: Osona
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic plain and early medieval county (Ausona) centered on Vic, derived from the pre-Roman Ausetani.

language_variants.notes: Late Antique and Carolingian Latin form

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Ausona in 6th-century CE Visigothic conciliar records (516 CE) and Carolingian charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from classical Ausa / Ausetani, the Iberian tribe inhabiting the central Catalan basin.

replacement_candidates.name: Mèder
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing directly through Vic before joining the Gurri and the Ter.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Local Osona hydronym attested in medieval Vic records; no classical attestation.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman or early medieval hydronym of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Latin root *med-.

replacement_candidates.name: Indigetes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe of the Empordà whose largest fortified oppidum (Puig de Sant Andreu) is located at Ullastret.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Avienius (drawing on earlier periploi), Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and on 2nd-century BCE Iberian coins inscribed Untikesken.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym from the base Untika / Indika (associated with Emporion/Empúries) + Iberian gentilic -sken.

replacement_candidates.name: Daró
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing past Ullastret across the Baix Empordà plain.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Empordà charters; reflects a pre-Roman Iberian/Mediterranean hydronym.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman hydronym likely from the widespread river root *dar-/*dur- ('water, watercourse').

replacement_candidates.name: Empordà
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic coastal plain and natural region of northeastern Catalonia encompassing Ullastret.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as the Carolingian County of Empúries (Emporitanus) by the early 9th century CE, derived from Greek Emporion (founded c. 575 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Latin Emporitanus, derived from Greek Emporion (Ἐμπόριον, 'trading post, market', modern Empúries).

replacement_candidates.name: Fluvià
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river flowing directly through Olot toward the Gulf of Roses.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Identified with the Clodianus attested by Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE) and later recorded as Fluvianus in early medieval Catalan charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from Latin fluvianus (from fluvius, 'river'), possibly reshaping the earlier Roman name Clodianus.

replacement_candidates.name: Garrotxa
replacement_candidates.relationship: Volcanic natural region and comarca of which Olot is the capital.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 10th-century CE Catalan documents (Garroxia / Garrotxa).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From pre-Roman/Catalan garrotxa ('rough, broken, rocky terrain'), derived from the pre-Indo-European root *kar-/*gar- ('stone, crag').

replacement_candidates.name: Castellani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe placed by Ptolemy in the Pre-Pyrenean interior corresponding to the Garrotxa and Ripollès around Olot.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested solely by Claudius Ptolemy in Geographia (c. 150 CE) as a people of northeastern Tarraconensis between the Ausetani and Ceretani.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Latinized ethnonym (from castellum, 'fortified hilltop settlement', or an Iberian root adapted to Latin).

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Steep hill (Latin acer mons, 'sharp/steep mountain')

replacement_candidates.name: Sió
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing directly through Agramunt on its way to the Segre.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Urgell charters (Sione / Sió); reflects a pre-Roman hydronym.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman hydronym of uncertain origin, possibly Iberian or pre-Indo-European *sione.

replacement_candidates.name: Urgell
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic Catalan plain and comarca containing Agramunt.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as the Diocese of Urgell (Urgellum) from the early 6th century CE (Bishop Justus, 527 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Pyrenean/Vasconic toponym, commonly linked to Basque ur ('water') + suffix -gel/-gell ('place of water').

replacement_candidates.name: Ilergetes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Iberian tribe inhabiting the Segre and Sió plains of Lleida and Urgell.

language_variants.notes: Iberian name of their capital, modern Lleida

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 218 BCE — Polybius (Histories 3.35) and Livy record the Ilergetes under Indibilis and Mandonius along the Cinca and Segre.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym linked to their capital Iltirta/Ilerda (from Iberian *iltir-, 'city/town', cf. Basque iri).

existing_natural_proper_name.name: High mountain meadows (Latin prata)

replacement_candidates.name: Siurana
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain river rising on the slopes directly below Prades and draining southward through Priorat to the Ebro.

language_variants.notes: Riu de Siurana; also 'Ciurana' — Traditional orthographic variant.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 12th-century CE Catalan/Andalusi records (Shibrana / Siurana).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Likely from a pre-Roman or Roman estate/hydronym *Severiana or *Suburana, adapted through Andalusi Arabic Shibrana.

replacement_candidates.name: Francolí
replacement_candidates.relationship: River whose headwaters rise in the Prades Mountains before flowing to Tarragona.

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Medieval Catalan Francolí (possibly from a Germanic/Frankish personal name or Latin diminutive *Francolinus); classical Tulcis is pre-Roman Iberian.

replacement_candidates.name: Cessetani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe inhabiting the Camp de Tarragona and the surrounding Prades uplands.

language_variants.notes: Iberian coin legend of their capital

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in accounts of the Second Punic War (218 BCE, Polybius/Livy) and on Iberian bronze coins inscribed Kese.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym derived from their chief city Kese (Cissa, near Tarraco) with the Latinized suffix -tani.

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Lower Pallars (Pyrenean valley)

replacement_candidates.name: Flamisell
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Pyrenean river draining the Vall Fosca through Pallars Jussà before joining the Noguera at La Pobla de Segur.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Regional Pyrenean hydronym attested in medieval Catalan charters of Pallars.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Uncertain; possibly from a pre-Roman Pyrenean hydronym or Latin *Flamicellus.

replacement_candidates.name: Montsec Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Limestone Pre-Pyrenean mountain range forming the southern wall of Pallars Jussà.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Catalan charters around 1000 CE as Monte Sicco / Montsec.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Catalan mont ('mountain') + sec ('dry', Latin mons siccus), describing the arid limestone ridge.

replacement_candidates.name: Ilergetes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Iberian people of the Lleida/Segre basin whose northern pre-Pyrenean sphere bordered and encompassed the Montsec and southern Pallars Jussà.

language_variants.notes: Iberian coin legend of their capital Ilerda (Lleida)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 218 BCE — Polybius (Histories 3.35) and Livy record the Ilergetes under Indibilis and Mandonius along the Cinca and Segre.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym derived from the root *iltir- ('town, settlement', cf. Iltirta/Ilerda, modern Lleida).

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Upper Pallars (Pyrenean valley)

replacement_candidates.name: Noguera de Cardós
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal high-Pyrenean valley river draining central Pallars Sobirà without embedding the post-867 Pallars name.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin form of the base hydronym Noguera

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Base hydronym Noguera (Nocaria) and valley name Cardós attested in 9th-century CE Urgell charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Noguera from pre-Roman/Pyrenean hydronym *Nocaria (folk-etymologized to Catalan noguera, 'walnut tree') + Cardós (Basque/Pyrenean oronymic root).

replacement_candidates.name: Pica d'Estats
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest mountain peak in Catalonia (3,143 m), located on the northern crest of Pallars Sobirà.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Pyrenean peak name recorded in early modern Catalan and French cartography (first documented ascent 1864 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Catalan pica ('sharp peak') + Estats (derived from Catalan/Occitan estatge, 'shepherd's summer dwelling/high pasture', or 'states' at the frontier).

replacement_candidates.name: Andosini
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Pyrenean people attested by Polybius between the Ebro and the Pyrenees (Andorra and adjacent upper Pallars/Alt Urgell valleys).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Polybius in Histories (3.35) among the Pyrenean peoples subdued by Hannibal in 218 BCE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Pyrenean/Vasconic ethnonym widely connected to Andorra (root *and- + Aquitanian/Iberian suffix -os-ini).

replacement_candidates.name: Val d'Aran
replacement_candidates.relationship: Atlantic-facing Pyrenean valley of which Vielha e Mijaran is the capital.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Pyrenean charters by the 10th–11th centuries CE (Vallis Aranensis).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Tautological compound of Romance val ('valley') + Basque/Aquitanian haran ('valley').

replacement_candidates.name: Garonne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing directly through Vielha (known locally as the Garona).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Garumna by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (58–50 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Indo-European/Aquitanian *gar-/*kar- ('rock, stone') + hydronymic suffix -onna/-umna (also associated with Gaulish *onna, 'river/spring').

replacement_candidates.name: Airenosis
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Pyrenean/Aquitanian people attested by Polybius, widely identified with the inhabitants of the Val d'Aran.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Polybius in Histories (3.35) as a Pyrenean people encountered by Hannibal in 218 BCE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Pyrenean/Aquitanian ethnonym commonly linked to Basque haran ('valley') and the Val d'Aran.

existing_natural_proper_name.name: Mont Cerdà ('hill of Cerdanya')

replacement_candidates.name: Ceretani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Pyrenean/Iberian tribe inhabiting the Cerdanya plateau and giving it its name.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Roman sources from the 1st century BCE (defeated by Domitius Calvinus in 39 BCE; described by Strabo and Pliny the Elder).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Pyrenean/Iberian ethnonym from which the regional name Cerdanya (Ceretania) derives.

replacement_candidates.name: Segre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing across Cerdanya directly past Puigcerdà.

language_variants.notes: classical Latin form attested by Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Sicoris by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Civili (49 BCE, Battle of Ilerda).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Latin Sicoris, a pre-Roman Iberian/Indo-European hydronym (*sik-/*seg-, 'stream, water').

replacement_candidates.name: Cerdanya
replacement_candidates.relationship: High Pyrenean tectonic valley of which Puigcerdà is the historic capital.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Ceretania in late antique and early medieval chronicles (e.g., 8th-century CE Carolingian/Mozarabic sources).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived directly from Latin Ceretania, the territory of the ancient Ceretani tribe.

replacement_candidates.name: Têt
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river of Roussillon flowing directly through Perpignan.

language_variants.notes: classical Latin form attested by Pomponius Mela

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Telis by Pomponius Mela (c. 43 CE) and as Tetis in early medieval Roussillon charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman hydronym Telis / Tetis, possibly from an Iberian or pre-Indo-European root.

replacement_candidates.name: Sordones
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Iberian people of Roussillon centered at Ruscino (Château-Roussillon, within modern Perpignan).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Pomponius Mela (c. 43 CE), Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE), and Avienius (Ora Maritima).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Iberian/Pyrenean ethnonym of the inhabitants of Roussillon, whose chief centers were Ruscino and Illiberis (Elne).

replacement_candidates.name: Canigó
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iconic Pyrenean mountain massif dominating the skyline of Perpignan and the Roussillon plain.

language_variants.notes: Pic du Canigou / Massif du Canigou

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 10th-century CE Catalan/Roussillon charters as Monte Canigone (949 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Pyrenean oronym *Kan-ik-one, likely from the pre-Indo-European root *kan-/*kar- ('rock, height').

replacement_candidates.name: Ebro
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Iberian river flowing immediately west of the Maials plateau.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 226 BCE — Ebro Treaty between Rome and Carthage (Polybius, Histories 2.13) establishes the Iberus as a geopolitical boundary.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Roman Iberian/Vasconic hydronym Iber/Hiberus (often compared to Basque ibar, 'valley/riverbank', or ibai, 'river'); gave its name to Iberia.

replacement_candidates.name: Segrià
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic natural region and comarca of southern Lleida encompassing Maials.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Catalan records following the 12th-century CE conquest of Lleida, referring to the lower Segre basin.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from the Segre river (Latin Sicoris) + Catalan adjectival/regional suffix -ià (-ianus).

replacement_candidates.name: Ilercavones
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iberian tribe of the lower Ebro whose northern frontier met the Ilergetes around Maials and the Garrigues.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested by Livy (for 218 BCE), Julius Caesar, and Pliny the Elder as the Iberian tribe of the lower Ebro.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Iberian ethnonym sharing the *iler-/*iltir- element with the Ilergetes (centered on Dertosa/Tortosa and the lower Ebro).

replacement_candidates.name: Indre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river flowing directly through Châteauroux (at its confluence with the Ringoire).

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin form (Gregory of Tours); also 'Andra' — Medieval Latin variant.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Gregory of Tours (6th century CE) as fluvium Angerem
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from a pre-Celtic or Gaulish hydronym *Angera / *Andera (later nasalized to Indre)

replacement_candidates.name: Champagne berrichonne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Open limestone plain natural region of central Berry in which Châteauroux is a principal urban center.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval and modern regional choronym for the open plains of central Berry
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Late Latin campania ('open flat country, plain') + Berrichon (< Bituriges)

replacement_candidates.name: Bituriges Cubi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Core Gaulish tribe of Berry inhabiting the Indre valley around Châteauroux and nearby Déols.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Caesar's Gallic Wars (52 BCE)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *bitu- ('world') + *rīges ('kings')

replacement_candidates.name: Creuse
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river flowing directly past Descartes (historically La Haye-en-Touraine), forming the Touraine–Poitou border.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin form (8th–13th century CE)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested from the 8th century CE as Crosa / Chrosa
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *crosa ('hollow, deep-cut channel'), referring to the river's incised valley

replacement_candidates.name: Esves
replacement_candidates.relationship: Right-bank tributary of the Creuse draining the northern edge of Descartes (La Haye).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Touraine toponyms (Civray-sur-Esves, Marcé-sur-Esves)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Likely derived from Gallo-Romance *eva / Latin aqua ('water, stream')

replacement_candidates.name: Turones
replacement_candidates.relationship: Gaulish tribe of Touraine (Indre-et-Loire) whose southern frontier reached La Haye-en-Touraine on the Creuse.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars (58–51 BCE)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Possibly from Proto-Celtic *turos ('strong, swift') or *turo- ('swelling, hill')

replacement_candidates.name: Bièvre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Sologne tributary of the Beuvron draining the Controis-en-Sologne area immediately around Contres.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Blésois charters; distinct from the Bièvre of Île-de-France.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Gaulish *bebros ('beaver') + hydronymic suffix -a, meaning 'beaver stream'

replacement_candidates.name: Sologne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Natural forested and sandy region (Sologne viticole / Grande Sologne) where Contres is located.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in early medieval records (6th–9th century CE) as Secalaunia
